newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Dissident Khmer Rouge welcomed into Cambodian army.
newsitem.headline: Dissident Khmer Rouge welcomed into Cambodian army.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen on Wednesday predicted Khmer Rouge hardliners would be wiped out by mid-1997 as 2,500 defectors from the hardline Maoist group were officially welcomed into the Cambodian army.
"I think by half (mid-) 1997, Anlong Veng will be finished," the second prime minister told Reuters shortly before a welcoming ceremony for the breakaway fighters.
Anlong Veng, located near the Thai border, is the jungle base of hardline guerrillas loyal to Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot.

Around 700 breakaway Khmer Rouge troops, representing the 2,500 defectors and 17,000 family members, received Cambodian army uniforms and new weapons in a ceremony at their northwestern base of Pailin that officially welded the former bitter enemies into the same fighting force.
"I am still a soldier, and I joined the Khmer Rouge army 20 years ago," said 70-year-old Chorn Reoun. "I am very pleased we have no more fighting ... and I will probably retire."
But Long Norin, an aide to breakaway leader Ieng Sary, said he believed hardline leader Pol Pot and his commanders Ta Mok and Son Senn were in Anlong Veng preparing to attack Pailin and Phnom Malai.
"But we don't believe they can beat us, because now we have joined the government already," he said.
Ei Chien, the breakaway Khmer Rouge commander of Pailin, appealed to the hardliners to also surrender their arms.

"May we seize this opportunity to appeal to our brother cadres and combatants and the dictatorial and fascist command of stubborn groups ... to stop spilling blood between Khmer and Khmer," he said in a statement.
Cambodian defence officials declined to estimate the number of remaining Khmer Rouge hardliners, but a Western military analyst put their ranks at about 2,000.

A second ceremony for several hundred more dissident guerrillas is planned for Thursday, when fighters from the nearby base of Phnom Malai will also trade in their Mao caps and worn fatigues for stiff new government-issue garb.

In August Ieng Sary's Pailin and Phnom Malai guerrillas broke with hardliners loyal to Pol Pot, whose brutal 1975-1979 regime was responsible for the deaths of more than one million Cambodians from starvation, disease or overwork.
Weeks of delicate negotiations ensued, with Cambodian co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen often competing to gain the upper hand, analysts said.

But in the end it was Hun Sen who recruited thousands of defectors directly to the government's ranks, cutting into Ieng Sary's potential base of support and leaving the rebel leader little bargaining power, analysts said.
Ei Chien steered clear of the spats in his statement, noting the former Khmer Rouge would not take on a political role in coming elections.
